intro: Bojnice draws its crowds for the fairytale castle, but one tree in the park beside it has survived longer than the building's own restorations. The Linden of King Matthias, tradition says planted in 1301, was close to dying by the 1950s and was rescued by two decades of surgery: dead wood cut away, cavities cleared and sealed, timber props under what was left. It is now eleven metres round, fenced off for its own protection, and still flowering every year under expert watch.
meta_description: The Linden of King Matthias in Bojnice, Slovakia: an 11-metre-round tree by legend planted in 1301, saved from near-death by decades of conservation work.
question_meta: Bojnice's mapped tree is the Linden of King Matthias, an 11-metre-round lime in the public castle park.
question_answer: Bojnice's mapped tree is the Linden of King Matthias (Lipa kráľa Mateja), a large-leaved lime in the public park beside Bojnice Castle. Tradition credits Matúš Čak of Trenčín with planting it in 1301, which is where the figure of over 700 years comes from, though Slovak sources themselves say current methods cannot establish its real age.
question_context: The tree stands in the castle's public park, free to walk even though the castle building and its zoo charge separate admission. By the early 1950s it was failing: small yellow-green leaves, weak flowering, and dieback serious enough that the castle museum's own account of the rescue reads like surgery. Restoration in 1952 and 1953 removed dead wood, cleared and sealed the cavities with clay and fungicide, and propped the remaining crown on timber supports; irrigation and root work followed in the 1990s. A 2015 statement from the museum director confirmed it was still flowering, and it is examined annually by specialists. The trunk is eleven metres round and the tree now stands nine metres tall with a five-metre crown, down from a historic 28 metres and a 36-metre spread. A linden propagated from it in 2005 had nearly caught up with its parent within ten years. The tree is fenced off and cannot be approached, a restriction dating to the 1950s conservation work.

faq.q: What is special about this tree?
faq.a: It is one of Slovakia's most famous trees by legend, tied to a 1301 planting date, and it survived a near-death decline in the 1950s thanks to two decades of conservation work that is still ongoing.

Tradition says over 700 years, from an unverified 1301 planting date. Slovak sources themselves note that current methods cannot establish the tree's real age, and at least one regional piece argues the legend has stretched it.

faq.q: Can I get close to the trunk?
faq.a: No. The tree has been fenced off since its 1950s restoration to protect it, so it can be viewed but not touched.
Yes, the castle park itself is free; only the castle building and its zoo charge separate admission.
A short walk from the Bojnice bus and rail stops to the castle park entrance.

trees.name: The Linden of King Matthias

location.address: Bojnice Castle park (Zámocký park), near the castle approach, Bojnice

trees.story:
A linden propagated from this tree in 2005 had nearly caught up with its parent ten years later. That says less about the sapling than about what is left of the mother. The trunk is eleven metres round and the tree above it is nine metres tall, with a crown spreading five. It once stood 28 metres high and threw its branches 36 metres across.

By the early 1950s it was close to finished. The leaves came out small and yellow-green, it barely flowered, and the castle museum's own account of the rescue reads like surgery: dead wood cut away, clay dug out of the cavities, fungicide, the holes sealed, timber props under what remained. That was 1952 and 1953. Irrigation and root work followed in the 1990s. In 2015 the museum director confirmed it was still flowering, and specialists examine it every year and report it in good condition. Seventy years of intensive care is the reason there is anything here to look at.

The famous age is inherited, not measured. Tradition has Matus Cak of Trencin planting it in 1301, which is where the figure of over 700 years comes from, and every tourist page in Slovakia repeats it. Slovak Wikipedia states that current methods cannot establish the tree's real age, and a regional paper has argued the legend stretched it considerably.

The tree stands fenced off in the castle park, for its own sake. You can look at it. You cannot walk up to it.

trees.access: Free; stands in the public castle park near the approach to Bojnice Castle (the castle building and zoo require separate paid tickets, the park itself does not). The tree is fenced off and visitors may not approach the trunk, a restriction put in place as part of its ongoing conservation since the 1950s; it can be viewed but not touched.
trees.transport: In the town of Bojnice; short walk from the Bojnice bus/rail stops to the castle park entrance
